key_insight: Combine smaller, cheaper draft trees with retrieval-augmented candidate expansion so speculative decoding keeps high acceptance rates without the VRAM and compute overhead of giant generated draft trees.
problem_solved: Large draft trees used to maximize speculative-decoding acceptance rates create severe VRAM bandwidth and compute bottlenecks; dynamic-depth pruning reduces latency but throws away valid candidates and prevents reaching the acceptance-rate upper bound.
method: Hybrid tree construction: build a compact generated draft tree and expand it with retrieved candidate continuations, prioritizing high-probability tokens while avoiding exhaustive generation.
Bandwidth- and acceptance-aware pruning: selectively prune marginal branches using a cost-aware heuristic so marginal branches are removed only when they harm end-to-end throughput, not acceptance.
Integrate retrieval into the draft-then-verify loop to recover candidate diversity lost by pruning, preserving acceptance rate while reducing VRAM/compute pressure.
impact: Enables faster, more resource-efficient LLM inference by achieving high speculative acceptance rates with much lower memory bandwidth and compute cost—beneficial for production deployments and hardware-constrained settings.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic: (a) large generated draft tree vs (b) hybrid tree + retrieval, showing fewer generated nodes but similar accepted outcomes.
Bar chart: end-to-end latency and VRAM bandwidth for baseline large-tree SD, dynamic-depth pruning, and hybrid method.
Flow diagram of the speculative-decoding loop: draft (generate + retrieve) → verify → accept/reject, highlighting where retrieval replaces extra generation.
Line plot: acceptance rate vs generated-draft-size showing hybrid method approaching the acceptance upper bound at much smaller draft sizes.
paper_title: Draft Less, Retrieve More: Hybrid Tree Construction for Speculative Decoding
paper_authors: Yuhao Shen, Tianyu Liu, Xinyi Hu, Quan Kong, Baolin Zhang
